ai_baseline_failures.description: The baseline AI's specific failures are what made the player's aggressive strategy possible. These failures are visible in the early telemetry and should inform any model's predictions.
ai_baseline_failures.deathball: All Red mechs moved as one blob. Spread=50 at start, briefly 343 at 1:03, collapsed back to 37 by end. Zero force distribution.
ai_baseline_failures.zero_waypoints: AI issued zero waypoints the entire game. No strategic deployment, no directed movement.
ai_baseline_failures.fsm_distribution: 72% capturing, 16% retaliate, 10% hunting, 2% wandering. The AI spent most of its time trying to capture nodes in a blob rather than fighting or scouting.
ai_baseline_failures.no_territory_response: Blue captured Red's base and Red didn't react for 75 seconds. No defense trigger, no redirect.
ai_baseline_failures.no_scouting: No scout behavior. No patrol. No information gathering. The AI never knew what the player was doing until the player arrived.
ai_baseline_failures.predictable_pathing: Red mechs plod forward in straight lines toward objectives. No flanking, no evasion, no terrain exploitation.
ai_baseline_failures.what_early_telemetry_reveals: In the first 6 minutes, a model should see: zero Red contacts at center, no Red movement toward center, Red spread values showing blob movement near Red base. These signals should drive the prediction that the human will push aggressively forward with no rear defense — because the AI is not threatening anything.

learning_trajectory.description: This session is Session 001 of a 5-session learning arc. The AI improved between sessions based on CC analyzing raw telemetry. The player also switched teams. This context matters because it shows what the same terrain and mechanics produce under different conditions.
learning_trajectory.session_001: Human=Blue vs naive Red. Blue won 6-1. Human used zero personal combat — pure deployment strategy.
learning_trajectory.session_002: Human=Blue vs improved Red (CC added split deployment, LOS-based territory awareness, scouting, anti-deathball). The AI learned from Session 001 telemetry.
learning_trajectory.session_003: Human=Red vs improved Blue. Player switched to the fast/fragile team against a Blue AI that had learned from watching a human play Blue. Player now facing their own strategy reflected back.
learning_trajectory.session_004: Human=Red vs further-improved Blue. AI adapted to Red playstyle.
learning_trajectory.session_005: Both trained AIs against each other. No human player. Both incorporating lessons from human play.
learning_trajectory.relevance_to_predictions: Session 001 is the baseline. The AI's failures in this session are KNOWN and DOCUMENTED because they were diagnosed and fixed for Session 002. The fixes themselves (split deployment, scouting, anti-deathball, territory awareness) are a catalog of what the baseline AI was NOT doing — and therefore what the player was exploiting.

overall_strategy_summary: Aggressive forward expansion. Blue player treated the game as a capture-speed race against passive AI. No defensive posture adopted at any point. Center was a waypoint, not a position to hold. Force multiplication through capture-spawn mechanic was the primary strategic lever.

micro_contexts.time_window_description: Early session — first 2-3 minutes. Center captured quickly with no resistance.
micro_contexts.question: After center is captured/contested, does the player distribute mechs around center for defense, concentrate all forces, or exploit the respawn-at-node advantage?
micro_contexts.ground_truth: Neither distributed nor concentrated for defense. Center was captured unopposed and immediately treated as a force multiplication point. The key insight: capturing center spawns heavy mechs RIGHT THERE — this is faster than walking them from Blue base. The player captured center not primarily for territorial control but because spawning heavy mechs at the geographic midpoint is more efficient than marching reinforcements across the map. Center was a production facility, not a defensive position. Player pivoted to forward expansion within seconds, now backed by freshly spawned heavies at center.
micro_contexts.dominant_cognitive_band: Command (8-30s). Quick capture decision driven by efficiency calculus (spawn here > walk from base), immediate pivot to next objective. The absence of defensive setup reveals two things: the player read the AI's passivity AND understood the capture-spawn mechanic as a logistics advantage, not just a territorial one.
key_behavioral_signals: No mechs left at center as garrison after capture
Waypoints set forward (toward Node 2) during or immediately after center capture
Short dwell time at center node — capture and move, not capture and hold
No radar checks backward after leaving center
Newly spawned heavy mechs at center used as forward force, not garrison
micro_contexts.what_models_will_likely_predict_wrong: Most models will predict defensive distribution or concentration at center because generic RTS doctrine says 'secure your gains.' They will also miss the efficiency reasoning — the player captured center because spawning heavy mechs there is faster than walking them from base. Models that describe capture as 'territorial control' are missing the logistics insight: capture-as-production, not capture-as-defense.

micro_contexts.time_window_description: Mid-session. After center capture, player pushed south toward Node 2 while setting waypoints for NPC mechs to rendezvous.
micro_contexts.question: Will the player prioritize capturing Node 2, Node 4, or neither? Which mountain node will they target first and why?
micro_contexts.ground_truth: Player went center first, then pushed toward Node 2 (eastern mountain, deeper into Red territory). Critically, the player set waypoints for NPC mechs to converge on Node 2 simultaneously — the tmech would arrive first (fastest unit), but allied mechs were already en route. This is a force multiplication play: arrive first at Node 2, capture it (spawning new mechs there), and be reinforced by the waypointed allies arriving shortly after. Node 2's position is also dual-purpose — it's close enough to center to provide support there OR to flank Red's forward positions. It's not just a forward base; it's a coverage geometry play. Node 4 was deliberately deprioritized — the player recognized that even if Red held Node 4, the fighting there would keep forces distributed, and the respawn mechanic meant recapture was always available.
micro_contexts.dominant_cognitive_band: Sustained (30s+). This decision involves parallel strategic reasoning: simultaneous forward push with tmech + waypoint coordination of NPC allies + deliberate acceptance of Node 4 as expendable. The layered reasoning (force multiplication through capture-spawn + rendezvous timing + acceptable loss calculus) is L3-L4 strategic cognition.
key_behavioral_signals: Waypoint events sent toward Node 2 area during or shortly after center capture
tmech movement trajectory: center → south/southeast toward Node 2
No waypoints or movement toward Node 4 in early-to-mid session
If Node 4 was contested later, player did not redirect main force — accepted distributed fighting
micro_contexts.what_models_will_likely_predict_wrong: Models may predict Node 4 first because it's closer to Blue's territory (safer choice). The ground truth reveals the player chose the aggressive deep option (Node 2) because the waypoint-rendezvous strategy made it viable — a prediction that requires understanding the capture-spawn mechanic, not just spatial proximity.

micro_contexts.time_window_description: Mid-to-late session. After securing center and pushing toward Node 2.
micro_contexts.question: Once the player pushes forward toward contested space, will they monitor rear nodes via radar checks, defend with dedicated mechs, or ignore rear entirely?
micro_contexts.ground_truth: Ignored rear nodes entirely during the forward push. Full forward pressure with no radar checks backward and no mechs dedicated to rear defense. The player assessed that Red was overwhelmed and had no capacity to threaten Blue's rear. This was correct — the naive AI stayed near its own territory and never mounted a flanking attack. The critical late-game insight: pushing toward Red's base, the player hit the RESPAWN WALL. The same capture-spawn mechanic that benefited Blue at center now PROTECTED Red at their base — Red mechs die and respawn right there within 5 seconds, making direct base assault effectively impossible through brute force. The correct play, which the player executed, was to send mechs AROUND Red's base to capture the unguarded nodes behind and beside it. Node 4, while somewhat of a diversion, serves as part of this encirclement. Red never figured out the respawn-wall defense was working for them — they just died and respawned without strategic intent. The player recognized the mechanic asymmetry: respawn-at-base is a passive defense that works even without strategic awareness. Additionally, the AI's pathing behavior is directly exploitable: Red mechs plod forward in predictable straight lines. The player exploited this by flanking from the side with ranged Blue mechs — Blue's longer weapon range means you can pick off AI mechs before they close to their own effective range. This requires patience (running around to the side rather than engaging head-on) but is low-risk because the AI doesn't adapt its heading. The combination of predictable AI pathing + Blue's range advantage + the respawn wall makes encirclement not just strategically correct but tactically easy.
micro_contexts.dominant_cognitive_band: Assess (2-8s) for the initial decision to ignore rear, then Sustained (30s+) for the late-game recognition of the respawn wall and the strategic pivot to encirclement. The key cognitive signals are: (1) what DIDN'T happen — no radar toggles backward, no defensive waypoints, no tab-switches to rear mechs; (2) the STRATEGIC PIVOT — recognizing that direct base assault fails against the respawn mechanic and switching to capturing unguarded nodes around the base instead. This is L4 metacognition: understanding that the game mechanic that helped you now helps your opponent, and adapting your approach accordingly.
key_behavioral_signals: Zero or near-zero radar toggles directed at Blue's rear territory during forward push
No tab-switches to mechs positioned near Node 5 or Blue base during mid-session
No defensive waypoints sent to rear positions
Late-session: repeated kills near Red base WITHOUT capture progress = respawn wall evidence
Waypoints sent AROUND Red base to unguarded rear nodes rather than continuing direct assault
Player-controlled mech positioning at oblique angles to AI advance direction = flanking with range advantage
Combat events showing Blue kills at distances beyond Red weapon range = range exploitation
The ABSENCE of rear-checking events is the signal — models must recognize that missing telemetry events carry diagnostic meaning
micro_contexts.what_models_will_likely_predict_wrong: Models trained on competitive RTS analysis will predict radar checks and rear defense because that's doctrinally correct. They will also predict a direct push to Red base as the endgame. The ground truth reveals two insights models will miss: (1) situational awareness includes knowing when NOT to check — the player's read of AI passivity eliminated the need for rear monitoring; (2) the respawn mechanic creates a defensive wall at base that requires encirclement, not assault. A model that predicts 'push to base and capture' doesn't understand the respawn mechanic. A model that predicts 'send forces around base to unguarded nodes' demonstrates systems-level reasoning about game mechanics.

meta_annotation.overall_cognitive_profile: Aggressive expansionist with deep mechanical reasoning. Player understood capture-spawn not as territorial control but as production logistics (spawning heavies at center is faster than walking them from base). Player used Node 2's position for dual-purpose coverage (support center OR flank). Late-game, player recognized the respawn-wall paradox — the same mechanic that powered Blue's expansion now defended Red's base — and adapted by encircling rather than assaulting. This is systems-level cognition: understanding that a game mechanic has different strategic implications depending on who benefits from it and when.
meta_annotation.what_makes_this_session_diagnostic: Four layers of mechanical reasoning that most AI models will miss: (1) capture-as-production, not capture-as-territory — spawning heavies at center is faster than marching them; (2) dual-purpose node positioning for coverage geometry — Node 2 supports center AND flanks; (3) respawn-wall recognition and the strategic pivot from assault to encirclement; (4) AI pathing exploitation — Red mechs plod forward predictably, Blue's range advantage lets the player flank from the side and pick them off before they can close. Each layer requires understanding the game as an interacting system of mechanics, not just applying RTS templates.
meta_annotation.the_respawn_wall: The defining late-game mechanic. Red mechs respawn at their base within 5 seconds of dying. Direct assault produces kills but never capture progress — the defenders regenerate faster than the attacker can clear them. The correct play is to bypass the base and capture unguarded nodes around it. A model that predicts direct base assault as the endgame doesn't understand this mechanic. A model that predicts encirclement demonstrates L4 systems reasoning.
meta_annotation.the_perimeter_trap: The terrain has passable low ground around the mountain perimeter. No experienced player uses it for general flanking because the nodes are on the mountains, not around them. However, the perimeter DOES become relevant in the late-game encirclement of Red base — sending mechs around rather than through. Models that predict perimeter flanking as a general strategy are wrong; models that predict it specifically for base encirclement are demonstrating contextual mechanical reasoning.
